title: Sex Differences in Neuroinflammation in Rodent Models of Parkinson’s Disease: A Systematic Review
content: This review asks whether female and male animals differ in neuroinflammatory measurements in Parkinson’s disease models and whether the findings establish different responses to disease induction. We searched APA PsycNET, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science and SciELO, initially covering publications from January 2014 to December 31, 2024. Update searches ran from May 12 to May 31, 2025. Eligible studies used neurotoxin, pesticide or genetic models in rodents or nonhuman primates and included both sexes and control groups. We assessed risk of bias with the Systematic Review Centre for Laboratory Animal Experimentation (SYRCLE) tool. Findings were tabulated and compared descriptively, accounting for shared cohorts and distinguishing differences in measured values from interactions involving sex. Variation in methods and measurements, incomplete numerical data and uncertain independence prevented pooling. Eighteen publications represented 17 study units, all in rodents. No nonhuman primate studies were eligible. A total number of unique animals could not be established. Among mice that underwent sham surgery without dutasteride, striatal glial fibrillary acidic protein fluorescence increased after 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP) in males; no increase was detected in females. An interaction between sex and MPTP exposure supported different responses. Microglial density and branching after rotenone varied with sex and genotype. Female mice overexpressing $\alpha$-synuclein had higher plasma interleukin 5 than males at 4 and 18 months. After a 6-hydroxydopamine lesion, male rats given a control oligonucleotide had more cells expressing inducible nitric oxide synthase per section in the substantia nigra pars compacta than females given the same treatment. These last two comparisons did not establish different responses to disease induction. Many findings relied on separate analyses within each sex. Unclear risk of bias, sparse replication and variation in assays and conditions limited interpretation. Some glial and inflammatory measurements differed between sexes under particular experimental conditions. The evidence does not establish generally greater neuroinflammation in either sex. Comparable independent experiments and direct assessment of cellular function are needed to clarify the biological significance of these differences.
